L’Express , a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind. data.title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip | Simon Tisdall
data.description: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country Imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population. Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians, Uyghurs and others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see as forced assimilation into a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name. Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator Continue reading...

data.title: Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answer
data.description: I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple The last time I opened X, a photo of Ariana Grande leaning over in a low-cut black dress, clavicle showing, was at the top of the feed. The post read: “hey @grok make Ariana Grande healthy and fat”. Images of celebrities at their most skeletal regularly rise to the top of social feeds because they generate enormous, dissenting engagement. Social media platforms have made half-hearted efforts to suppress explicit pro-eating disorder content; Instagram and TikTok redirect searches for “ thinspo ” toward support resources. Yet over the past couple weeks, Grande has sent users into a frenzy that outstrips the platforms’ attempts. Continue reading...

data.title: The night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfolded
data.description: A horrific knife attack on a street in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again? Shortly after 10.30pm on Monday 8 June, as a summer twilight lingered over Belfast, a horrific scene unfolded on Kinnaird Avenue: a man straddled and repeatedly stabbed a figure lying on the ground in a bloody assault that ended only after onlookers intervened. Others captured the drama on cameraphones and uploaded the footage to social media. Once seen, the grainy images were hard to forget, and by dawn on Tuesday 9 June they were ricocheting around X, WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and other platforms. Continue reading...

data.title: Cockroach protests: parents of Indian students who took their own lives reveal pressure of leaked exam papers and resits
data.description: The number of student suicides in the country has risen steeply in the past 10 years and many families blame education system mismanagement as a contributing factor When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks. The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students. Continue reading...

data.title: Ukraine war briefing: Turkey calls for ‘moratorium’ on Black Sea attacks by Russia and Ukraine
data.description: Commercial ships under attack as Russia-Ukraine conflict spreads across Black Sea, says Turkey’s foreign minister. What we know on day 1,626 Turkey’s foreign minister on Saturday called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there. “The conflict has spread across the whole Black Sea,” Hakan Fidan said in an interview with Turkey’s state news agency Anadolu. “To begin with, they targeted the ports and the military ships. Now, they are attacking all commercial shipping without distinction,” he added. Ships belonging to Turkey or flying the Turkish flag were among those targeted, he said. Russia has continued ⁠striking Ukrainian port infrastructure and vessels supporting the Ukrainian ⁠military , Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday. The ministry ⁠said Russian forces hit military warehouses ‌containing communications and electronic warfare equipment in the Black Sea port of Odesa. In the port of Mykolaiv, Russian forces ‌struck a cargo vessel carrying military equipment and ​a warehouse storing weapons and military supplies, the ministry said. It added that another dry ⁠cargo vessel transporting military supplies ​for Ukraine’s ​armed forces ​was hit in the ​Black ‌Sea. Ukraine on Saturday denied targeting Bulgaria after a drone exploded close to the strategic Trans-Balkan gas pipeline linking Turkey to Ukraine near the Romanian border. There were no casualties or damage. Bulgaria’s defence ministry said the drone was of a type “widely used by the Ukrainian military”, and the foreign minister summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for a meeting on Monday in response, her office told AFP. Kyiv said it was “in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances” of the incident, the latest case of a drone straying into Nato airspace as Ukraine fights off Russia’s invasion. “We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria,” Ukraine’s foreign ministry spokesperson Georgiy Tykhyi said, blaming Russia’s invasion for the incident. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned Ukraine is facing a winter with no working thermal power plants as overnight Russian strikes left four dead, including a child, in the Kyiv region. Speaking Saturday in Belgrade, alongside his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vucic, the Ukrainian leader said Moscow’s latest overnight attacks and shelling of frontline communities combined had killed 13 people in the last 24 hours. “Russian missiles are aimed precisely at making the lives of Ukrainians unbearable,” Zelensky told reporters during his first official visit to Belgrade. Zelenskyy is in Serbia for talks on economic ties and security issues. The visit, which included talks with President Vucic on Saturday, is the first by a Ukrainian president in eight years. Vucic described Ukraine as a “friendly nation” and said he was honoured to welcome the Ukrainian leader. The two men discussed their countries’ efforts to join the European Union, bilateral ties and ways to expand cooperation. Drones have been detected above an army installation in western Germany known to house components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems , which Ukraine has frequently requested to help fight off Russia’s aerial bombardments. An investigation has been opened into the sighting at the installation, which has a large underground depot, a military operational command spokesperson said on Saturday. Mechernich is a special army site for storing equipment at a depth of 130 metres (425 feet) across about 30,000 square metres, or the equivalent of four football pitches. The latest incident comes days after an explosives-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig-Halle airport, which plays a key role in the transport of military goods by the German military and Nato allies. Continue reading...

data.title: Blame game as Brussels builds ‘Europe’s largest frying pan’ instead of shady square
data.description: Architect’s vision for redevelopment of heart of EU quarter unrealised amid political wrangling and rising costs The redevelopment plan for Schuman Square at the heart of the EU quarter in Brussels was very ambitious. From a traffic-clogged, nondescript roundabout, it would become “an urban agora”, a greener, calmer meeting place, nothing less, said a former head of the Brussels government, than “a symbol that beats as the heart … of the European project”. It did not turn out that way. The result, say critics, is Europe’s largest frying pan, a concrete expanse with little greenery or shade. While the number cars has reduced and the space is remodelled with smart grey paving, the centrepiece – a steel canopy with a green roof – was never built. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘They kidnapped a hard-working kid off our streets’: the gardener seized by ICE – and the New York town fighting back
data.description: Gerson Turcios was 17 when he fled violence in Honduras to build a new life in the US. Six years later, he was mowing lawns in his home town of Rhinebeck when immigration officers took him. Within hours, friends, neighbours and local celebrities sprang into action. Could they stop his deportation? Gerson Turcios didn’t recognise the men standing next to a couple of dark SUVs outside his house one July afternoon last year. He figured they were lost and approached to see if he could help. A slim 23-year-old with short dark hair and big brown eyes, Turcios had just finished work mowing lawns in the pretty town of Rhinebeck, in New York’s Hudson Valley. The men asked if he knew someone called Jimmy – he did, but Jimmy hadn’t lived in the small, white weatherboard house with Turcios, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend for a while. The men noted Turcios’s accent and asked where he was from. Turcios didn’t answer, so one took out his phone and snapped a photograph. The next thing Turcios knew, he was in handcuffs in the back of one of the SUVs and on his way to an ICE processing centre in Newburgh, New York, then on to a detention centre. Continue reading...

data.title: Bullgogi, Manchester M1: ‘Highly decent, amenable, human-free dining’ – restaurant review
data.description: Bullgogi’s largely automated hospitality will either delight or horrify you, but the food is serious Bullgogi , a whopping new interactive multiscreen Korean restaurant in Manchester’s Piccadilly Plaza, has arrived, heralding the end of traditional hospitality – again. It’s the UK’s largest Korean barbecue restaurant – 165 covers, traditional tabletop grills at every booth – but has no servers with notepads, just screens. Your gyeran jjim , your dolsot bibimbap , your bulgogi : jab the at-table screen and it will arrive, ferried by human hand. Think McDonald’s, but as a gargantuan restaurant. Jae Cho and his Maguro Group have built an empire of 21 locations across London and Manchester, but this is their biggest venture to date. We arrive without reservation, which is no problem, because Bullgogi is the size of a small planet. We order pots of barley tea and pints of Asahi at £6.90, and sit back to enjoy the Blade Runner vibes. Bullgogi’s largely human-free hospitality will either delight or horrify you. Personally, I greet our new robot hospitality overlords with calm scepticism. Over the past few decades, I have staggered through the Covid QR menu wilderness, prised my dinner from the temperamental jaws of robot fridges in rural farm shops, and watched with mirth as the robot chef at a recent Soho yakitori joint still required a human to load every skewer into it before performing. For these reasons, I greet Bullgogi with a raised eyebrow. In fact, the moment we flag, via the screen, a food intolerance at our table, a bright, chipper human appears immediately to check through the menu for said offending item. Continue reading...

data.title: My husband won’t make any effort to please me in bed | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
data.description: This may be more to do with ageing than a lack of love. Talk about it – hopefully you can work out a new repertoire together My husband and I have been together for six years. He is 60, 20 years older than me . We had a baby last year and went through a really difficult time in our relationship. Things are better after some couples therapy, but we are both still unhappy with our sex life. I take a while to orgasm, and he gets very impatient and essentially just gives up (he always orgasms first, and quickly). I also have longstanding health issues that make sex painful. He has always been respectful when I say I can’t have sex because of the pain. But he gets defensive and unkind when I ask him to try new things to give me pleasure. He bought sex toys and says these were his way of trying, but I saw them as a way of him passing off a job he can’t be bothered to do. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriter
data.description: The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it This week, indie star Phoebe Bridgers releases her long-awaited third album, six years since her pandemic-era breakthrough. Alongside a slew of glittering reviews for Lost Weekend, including five stars from the Guardian , with it comes her first solo charting single in the UK – although the Californian musician’s influence runs far deeper than reviews or record sales could measure. Just how did a RuneScape-referencing, Halloween-costumed Berklee drop-out become the most influential songwriter of the 2020s? Bridgers’ idiosyncratic writing has shaped the sound of the decade. Her second album Punisher, released in June 2020 (and recorded many months before), spookily anticipated that strange, lonely year: in her eerie double-tracked vocals (a nod to Bridgers’ musical hero, Elliott Smith), Bridgers sang of empty shopping malls and conspiracy theories over lush, unsettling music made from watery electric guitar, Mellotron, strings, screams and birdsong. Today, Bridgers’ distinctive mix of dry wit and pathos is traceable in the lyrics of pop’s new chart toppers, such as Olivia Rodrigo and Gracie Abrams , while heavyweights across generations and genres, including Paul McCartney, Taylor Swift and SZA, have clamoured for collaborations. “She is the reference now,” Swift told the Guardian in 2022 . data.title: This burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadly | Sadiq Khan
data.description: Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth Report: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oil Europe is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves has swept through the continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods. With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuations in Suffolk and the Cairngorms . In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. With thousands of deaths already estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still. Sadiq Khan is mayor of London Continue reading...

data.title: Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa Mahdawi
data.description: An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming Robert F Kennedy Jr’s new cooking show isn’t the only big news out of the public health world this week. On Wednesday, Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), making her the first Black woman to hold the position. This is the first time in almost a year that the agency has had a permanent leader; the previous director, Susan Monarez, only lasted 29 days before she was ousted for butting heads with RFK about US vaccine policies. Translation: she was a little too keen on following accepted science for the Trump administration. So is Schwartz an RFK-approved vaccine skeptic who thinks you can cure cancer by praying to trees? Surprisingly: no. Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, actually has government experience and a public health background. During her confirmation hearing in July, she walked a careful tightrope when asked about her stance towards vaccines. Schwartz said she “will never betray the science” but also dodged questions about how she would handle pressure from Kennedy. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

data.title: Parenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us? | Dave Schilling
data.description: Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this? What job in our world is less lucrative than being a parent? A Hollywood internship? Volunteering at a soup kitchen? Professional writer? Parenting is the only job you have to pay money to do. Lots of money . Lodging, clothes, food, school, Pokémon cards – it really adds up. And it’s getting worse. According to the tech industry, I have to strap my drooling offspring to a computer in order to ensure the baby’s survival. Parents are being offered life-altering advancements in artificial intelligence that purport to make this taxing endeavor a tiny bit easier. OpenAI is suggesting its latest products can make child-rearing more efficient: its boss, Sam Altman, suggests generating a podcast about your kid’s life that you can listen to in the morning on the way to school. How entertaining would a podcast “that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc” actually be? “Jimmy needs to work on his dribbling.” Great. I think he knows already. He’s not going to be the next Messi, so how about we switch back to music? Continue reading...

data.title: West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay away
data.description: In an unseasonable black bomber jacket, with heavy duty company beside him, David Sullivan took his seat. Against the advice of the stadium’s operators, unbowed by serious allegations placed against his name and the weight of public opinion, West Ham’s major shareholder, the former co-chair, sat with arms crossed, always conspicuous by his presence. By beating Portsmouth in relative comfort, West Ham, the club where Sullivan’s name is no longer above the door, had secured a heartening Carabao Cup passage to the second round. There, they will be reunited with their former Premier League peers. The serious Championship business begins next Sunday at Burnley. Whether Sullivan travels north for that remains to be seen. It cannot be ruled out. Continue reading...

data.title: High divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s water
data.description: European Aquatics Championships taking place in city Threat to water quality tested two years after Games Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower – a spectacular new test of the city’s effort to reclaim its river for sport. The event on the Pont de Bir-Hakeim has also exposed the fragility of that ambition. Organisers suspended training on Thursday when traces of hydrocarbons were detected upstream. By Friday, the French Swimming Federation said the affected area had been treated, allowing athletes to return to the water and the event to proceed as planned. High diving concludes on Saturday with the final two rounds and medal events, while the broader European Aquatics Championships run through to 16 August. Continue reading...

data.title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs
data.description: Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start 2026-27 led by people with under a year in their dugout Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League. Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick – confirmed in March and May respectively – means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low. Continue reading...

data.title: A kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreams
data.description: The protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give up Explore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026 I was 28 the first time I did standup. It was an open-mic competition where the audience decided the winner. As I held the tiny gold trophy, I decided to quit my job the next day. Some people might call that crazy, and it probably was. But I’d been honing that delusional self-belief since I was eight when I first watched the film adaptation of Frances Hodgson Burnett’s story A Little Princess. I already almost had the same name as its protagonist, Sara, a young girl who is sent off to boarding school while her father fights in the war. I wanted to be exactly like her. She was so sure of herself, and believed so completely in the worlds she created, that all the other girls at school wanted to be her friend. My favourite scene is the one where the girls sit on Sara’s bed, forming a circle round her as she tells fantastical stories. I would watch it and think: I want to tell stories that make people gather round me. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad King
data.description: New play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelled A winter of discontent is anticipated by the embattled characters in Game of Thrones, but the Royal Shakespeare Company is banking on a glorious summer with its world premiere of a prequel to the hit TV series based on George RR Martin’s fantasy novels. The new play, The Mad King , arrives 30 years to the month after the original publication of A Game of Thrones, the first novel in Martin’s series A Song of Ice and Fire. It has a gala performance in Stratford-upon-Avon on Saturday evening in a reconfigured Royal Shakespeare theatre with a capacity of 870. data.title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
data.description: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back? If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life. AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant. Continue reading...

data.title: Sex, drugs and washing dishes: inside Anthony Bourdain’s unruly younger years
data.description: In the acclaimed new drama Tony, the early career of the late food writer and chef is brought to life, and those who knew him best are now also looking back The novelist Michael Cunningham has described Provincetown , on the tip of Cape Cod, as “the only small town I know of where those who live unconventionally seem to outnumber those who live within the prescribed bounds of home and licensed marriage, respectable job, and biological children. It is one of the places in the world you can disappear into.” This idiosyncratic bohemia has attracted the likes of Edward Hopper, Eugene O’Neill, Mark Rothko and Tennessee Williams along with poets, dropouts, drag queens and drifters. In the summer of 1975 came a lanky, restless 19-year-old from New Jersey with no job and no money, sleeping on the floor of a shared cottage while his roommates worked to pay the rent. His name was Anthony Bourdain , who would later become a celebrity chef, author and television globetrotter. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘You can feel the warmth of the sun’: Bertram Greenhough’s best phone picture
data.description: The Brighton-based photographer was walking along a crowded beach looking for ice-cream when he spotted this calm, minimalist scene Bertram Greenhough had promised his six-year-old daughter Audrey an ice-cream. It was a warm June day in Brighton and the pair were playing tourists in their own city, having just visited an upside-down house near the i360 observation tower. The beach was packed, and they were heading in the direction of the Palace Pier so that Greenhough could stay true to his word. Along the way, they passed this lifeguard shelter. “I often walk around Brighton with my SLR film camera – very hipster of me. However, that day I only had my phone,” Greenhough recalls. “But, as the adage goes, the best camera is the one you have with you. I saw this calm, minimalist scene suspended above thousands of people and I remember saying to my daughter, ‘Oh, look at that, I need to take a picture!’ She had no idea what I was talking about!” Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I haven’t felt this present for months’: sail back in time on a Thames barge in Essex
data.description: You don’t have to be a sailor to cruise the estuaries of Essex on this historic craft. The skipper will show you the ropes – or just sit back and enjoy the ride In a darkened room in Maldon, Essex, a ship’s lantern illuminates the laundry drying on a web of ropes suspended from the ceiling. Between piles of sailing memorabilia, 86-year-old Barry Pearce is flipping through a yellowing logbook, watched by his mongrel, Winkle. It feels more like a ship’s cabin than a terrace house. Pearce is one of a handful of surviving skippers who delivered freight on the Thames by sailing barge, the flat-bottomed trading boats famous for their striking red sails that were endemic to the river’s estuary until the 1960s. He remembers the names of every vessel he worked on – Remercie, Edith May, Colonia. In the 19th century, the ochre sails of thousands of Thames sailing barges pierced the skyline as the craft carried cargo from the Thames estuary and beyond in and out of London. Their shallow draft allowed them to snake far upriver in as little as a metre of water (bargemen would boast that they could sail anywhere there had been a heavy dew). Their ingenious rig, with sails that could be set and stowed with the help of winches, meant around 150 tonnes of cargo could be shifted by just a skipper and mate – often accompanied by a guard dog. This efficiency allowed them to outlive all other commercial sailing vessels, surviving until the 1960s, when Pearce himself took the helm. Continue reading...

data.title: A moth outbreak has killed off forests across Siberia, now the flammable wood is causing wildfires
data.description: In a catastrophic turn of events, a diminutive moth has decimated vast stretches of Siberian forest, transforming them into a fire hazard of monumental proportions. The Siberian silk moth's caterpillar stage ravages tree needles, resulting in widespread die-offs over several years. Major outbreaks have persisted over the decades, decimating millions of hectares, and now this ecological calamity aligns with an urgent wildfire emergency that has meteorological implications.

data.title: Florida's millions of dumped tyres are still being cleaned up 50 years later
data.description: Florida is set to embark on an ambitious initiative to clear millions of old tires that were dumped offshore decades ago. Initially forming an artificial reef, these tires have since led to significant damage to natural coral ecosystems. Present surveys indicate that over half a million tires still litter thousands of acres.

data.title: Meet Costa Rica's tiny 'coffee frog,' a nocturnal species found living among coffee shrubs
data.description: A remarkable discovery in Costa Rica reveals a diminutive nocturnal frog inhabiting the coffee plantations. Measuring less than four centimeters, this unique species relies on small insects for food and foliage for protection. Essential to its lifecycle are local streams, which face risks from pesticide runoff. This finding not only emphasizes the rich biodiversity in agricultural settings but also the urgent need for conservation initiatives.

data.title: 2-year-old sister becomes perfect bone marrow match for Utah girl with aplastic anemia
data.description: Emma Meline, a young girl diagnosed with severe aplastic anemia right before Christmas, found hope in her little sister Lucy. At only two years old, Lucy bravely became a bone marrow donor, granting Emma the chance for a life-saving transplant. After a challenging journey, Emma celebrated her fifth birthday at home, marking a remarkable recovery. This profound experience deepened the unbreakable bond between the two sisters.

data.title: EN DIRECT, guerre en Ukraine : après l’explosion en Bulgarie d’un drone correspondant à ceux utilisés par Kiev, l’ambassadrice ukrainienne à Sofia convoquée

La diplomatie ukrainienne a, de son côté, assuré que la Bulgarie n’avait pas été visée « délibérément », promettant une enquête pour expliquer cette chute.
data.translatedTitle: LIVE, war in Ukraine: after the explosion in Bulgaria of a drone corresponding to those used by kyiv, the Ukrainian ambassador in Sofia summoned
data.translatedDescription: The machine that crashed Saturday morning in Bulgaria is of a type “widely used by the Ukrainian armed forces,” announced Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov. Ukrainian diplomacy, for its part, assured that Bulgaria had not been “deliberately” targeted, promising an investigation to explain this fall.

data.title: Divulgação de arquivos do partido nazista abala histórias familiares na Alemanha
data.description: O representante de vendas de produtos médicos Stefan Dimter, 48, sempre ouviu do pai que seu avô nunca quis se envolver com política. Porém, após os arquivos de filiação do partido nazista terem sido divulgados pelo governo americano , essa narrativa foi posta em xeque. Ele nunca chegou a conhecer o avô, já que o comerciante nascido na região dos Sudetos, no antigo Império Austro-Húngaro, morreu antes dele nascer. Mas o nome de seu antecessor constava em uma das fichas como um membro do NSDAP (sigla em alemão para Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei, ou Partido Nacional-Socialista dos Trabalhadores Alemães). "Para mim, ainda não faz sentido. Mesmo agora falando isso, não entra na minha cabeça. Então, tento encontrar explicações." Leia mais (08/08/2026 - 23h00)
data.translatedTitle: Release of Nazi party files shakes family stories in Germany

However, after the Nazi party membership files were released by the American government, this narrative was called into question. He never got to know his grandfather, as the merchant born in the Sudetenland region, in the former Austro-Hungarian Empire, died before he was born. But his predecessor's name appeared on one of the records as a member of the NSDAP (acronym in German for Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei, or National Socialist German Workers' Party). "To me, it still doesn't make sense. Even now saying it, it doesn't enter my head. So I try to find explanations." Read more (08/08/2026 - 23:00)

data.translatedDescription: Here you will find today's highlights from DN's calendar, selected by DN's Anders Haraldsson. And here is the full calendar.

data.title: Högervindarna bland unga mojnar: ”Folk har det tufft”
data.description: Om unga väljare fått bestämma hade oppositionen vunnit valet, visar DN/Ipsos senaste mätningar. När DN pratar med unga väljare lyfter de fram flera möjliga förklaringar till opinionsvändningen – från kriminalpolitik till sociala medier. – När jag pratat med mina vänner så har inte vi varit särskilt nöjda med regeringen, säger Nicole Permansson.
data.translatedTitle: The right wing among young youths: "People have it tough"
data.translatedDescription: If young voters had decided, the opposition would have won the election, DN/Ipsos' latest surveys show. When DN talks to young voters, they highlight several possible explanations for the change in opinion - from criminal policy to social media. - When I talked to my friends, we were not particularly satisfied with the government, says Nicole Permansson.

data.title: Unga väljare har rört sig vänsterut
data.description: De unga väljarna har rört sig vänsterut sedan förra valet. Det visar en analys av DN/Ipsos opinionsdata. Oppositionspartierna har vunnit mark brett i flera väljargrupper – men det finns undantag.
data.translatedTitle: Young voters have moved to the left
data.translatedDescription: The young voters have moved to the left since the last election. This is shown by an analysis of DN/Ipsos opinion data. The opposition parties have gained ground widely in several voter groups - but there are exceptions.

data.title: Sakerna som gör svensken lycklig
data.description: Personlighet och sociala relationer har större betydelse för vårt välbefinnande än hur mycket vi tjänar. Ett specifikt personlighetsdrag sticker dock ut och är betydligt mer avgörande än andra. – Att må bra är ju en av de viktigaste sakerna som finns här i livet, säger forskaren August Nilsson.
data.translatedTitle: The things that make Swedes happy
data.translatedDescription: Personality and social relationships are more important to our well-being than how much we earn. However, one specific personality trait stands out and is far more decisive than others. - Feeling good is one of the most important things in life, says researcher August Nilsson.

data.title: Tom Alandh: Om man verkligen vill förstå meningen med livet så ska man åka kommunalt
data.description: Min resa i Stockholms tunnelbana började 1955. Jag har lärt mig att parera vartenda knyck och ryck och inbromsning – och mer än så. SOMMARRÖSTER. Under sommaren bjuder ledarredaktionen in några av sina favoritskribenter att breda ut sig i valfritt ämne. Tom Alandh är journalist och dokumentärfilmare.
data.translatedTitle: Tom Alandh: If you really want to understand the meaning of life, you should go by public transport
data.translatedDescription: My journey in the Stockholm subway began in 1955. I have learned to parry every jolt and jolt and braking - and more than that. SUMMER VOICES. During the summer, the editors invite some of their favorite writers to expand on a topic of their choice. Tom Alandh is a journalist and documentary filmmaker.

data.title: The Weeknd vill ge världens fläskigaste arenashow – men går vilse
data.description: Världsartistens första spelning i Stockholm är som att befinna sig mitt i ett lätt dystopiskt nöjesfält, skriver DN:s recensent.
data.translatedTitle: The Weeknd wants to give the world's porkiest arena show - but gets lost
data.translatedDescription: The world artist's first gig in Stockholm is like being in the middle of a slightly dystopian amusement park, writes DN's reviewer.

data.title: Svenska ”spökraketer” i amerikanska Pentagonfiler
data.description: Gryniga filmer, de flesta tagna från amerikanska militärplan, men även svenska ”spökraketer”, ingår i Pentagons femte släpp av filer om oidentifierade flygande föremål.
data.translatedTitle: Swedish "ghost rockets" in American Pentagon files
data.translatedDescription: Grainy footage, mostly taken from American military planes, but also Swedish "ghost rockets", is included in the Pentagon's fifth release of files on unidentified flying objects.

data.title: Nathan Shachar: Planerade regimskifte i Iran – nu offras agenterna av Netanyahu
data.description: De israeliska underrättelseagenter som planerade den iranska regimens fall efter krigsutbrottet den 28 februari har tvingats avgå. Den nye chefen för Mossad, Roman Gofman, fattade beslutet, som väckt utbredd indignation, också inom underrättelsetjänsterna.
data.translatedTitle: Nathan Shachar: Planned regime change in Iran - now the agents are sacrificed by Netanyahu
data.translatedDescription: The Israeli intelligence agents who planned the fall of the Iranian regime after the outbreak of war on February 28 have been forced to resign. The new head of Mossad, Roman Gofman, made the decision, which caused widespread indignation, also within the intelligence services.

data.title: Vänstersvängen en reaktion på Trump – men kan stå Demokraterna dyrt
data.description: En vänstervåg drar fram i det demokratiska partiet i USA. Bakom den finns ett starkt missnöje med Donald Trump – och växande kritik mot landets stöd till Israel. Men trenden riskerar att stå partiet dyrt i det stundande mellanårsvalet. – Risken är att vänstervågen skrämmer bort mittenväljarna, säger Dag Blanck.
data.translatedTitle: The left turn is a reaction to Trump - but could cost the Democrats dearly
data.translatedDescription: A left-wing wave is advancing in the Democratic Party in the United States. Behind it is a strong dissatisfaction with Donald Trump - and growing criticism of the country's support for Israel. But the trend risks costing the party dearly in the upcoming midterm elections. - The risk is that the left-wing wave scares away the middle voters, says Dag Blanck.

data.title: 8 augusti: Missa inte dagens nyheter
data.description: Svårt för många äldre att använda bank-id, kvinnohat fick henna att hoppa av extremhögern och arven blir allt större – här är nyheterna du inte får missa från dagen.
data.translatedTitle: August 8: Don't miss today's news
data.translatedDescription: It is difficult for many elderly people to use a bank ID, misogyny made her quit the extreme right and the inheritance is getting bigger - here are the news you can't miss from the day.

data.title: DN Debatt. ”Samernas historia är också Sveriges historia”
data.description: DN DEBATT. Vi har granskat konsekvenserna för samer av den politik som förts och förs i Sverige. Och talat med dem det berör. De berättar om rädsla, förluster och okunskap. Men också om styrka och vördnad inför marken där förfäderna vandrat. Nu måste Sverige lyssna, skriver Sanningskommissionen för det samiska folket.
data.translatedTitle: DN Debate. "The history of the Sami is also the history of Sweden"
data.translatedDescription: DN DEBATE. We have examined the consequences for the Sámi of the policies that have been and are being carried out in Sweden. And spoke to those concerned. They tell of fear, loss and ignorance. But also about strength and reverence for the land where the ancestors walked. Now Sweden must listen, writes the Truth Commission for the Sami people.

data.title: Max Hjelm: Har dagens föräldrar glömt bort sina barn?
data.description: Politiker gynnar gärna vuxna på ungas bekostnad: Från bostadspolitiken och anställningsskyddet, via valfläsk till sänkta klimatambitioner.
data.translatedTitle: Max Hjelm: Have today's parents forgotten their children?
data.translatedDescription: Politicians like to favor adults at the expense of young people: From housing policy and employment protection, via electoral pork to lowered climate ambitions.

data.title: Larmar: Föråldrad lagstiftning bromsar bilpooler
data.description: Föråldrad lagstiftning hindrar kommuner från att reservera parkeringsplatser för bilpooler, vilket bromsar omställningen till ett mer hållbart resande. Det slår Trafikutredningsbyrån fast i en ny rapport. – Lagstiftningen är skriven på 50-talet och tog aldrig höjd för det här, säger Pelle Envall, utredare på konsultfirman Trafikutredningsbyrån.
data.translatedTitle: Alarms: Outdated legislation slows down carpooling
data.translatedDescription: Outdated legislation prevents municipalities from reserving parking spaces for car pools, which slows down the transition to more sustainable travel. This is confirmed by the Traffic Investigation Agency in a new report. - The legislation was written in the 50s and never took this into account, says Pelle Envall, investigator at the consulting firm Trafiktredningsbyrån.

data.title: Havsfyndet – 162 år gammal Guinness
data.description: När belgaren Stefan Panis dök vid ett skeppsvrak utanför Dovers kust hittade han en mystisk flaska. Den visade sig vara en oöppnad Guinness från 1864 – och nu hoppas forskare kunna återskapa den historiska drycken.
data.translatedTitle: The sea find - 162-year-old Guinness
data.translatedDescription: When Belgian Stefan Panis dived at a shipwreck off the coast of Dover, he found a mysterious bottle. It turned out to be an unopened Guinness from 1864 - and now researchers are hoping to recreate the historic drink.

data.title: Svårt för många äldre att använda bank-id: ”En otrolig oro”
data.description: Frågan om bank-id och äldre är ett stort problem. Det vittnar flera aktörer och läsare om efter DN:s artikel om en 96-årig kvinna som fick sitt bank-id spärrat. Anhöriga till äldre uppger att de begår lagbrott för att få det att fungera. – För många är det här ett påtagligt problem, säger juristen Fredrik Nordquist.
data.translatedTitle: Difficult for many elderly people to use bank ID: "An incredible worry"
data.translatedDescription: The issue of bank ID and the elderly is a big problem. Several actors and readers testify to this after DN's article about a 96-year-old woman who had her bank ID blocked. Relatives of the elderly say they are breaking the law to make it work. - For many, this is a tangible problem, says lawyer Fredrik Nordquist.

data.title: Uttorkade floder kan radera Tysklands tillväxt 2026

data.translatedTitle: Dried up rivers could wipe out Germany's growth in 2026
data.translatedDescription: Germany's biggest rivers have dropped to record low levels after the summer's drought. Now the industry is warning that the low water could wipe out the country's growth this year.

data.title: Iransk attack mot tanker – samtalen fortsätter
data.description: Samtalen om Hormuzsundet går i positiv riktning, säger Omans förhandlare. Iran uppger åter att ett avtal är nära, men samtidigt säger man att ett öppet sund kräver att USA kompenserar Iran för brott mot avtalet som slöts i juni.
data.translatedTitle: Iranian attack on tanks - talks continue
data.translatedDescription: Talks on the Strait of Hormuz are moving in a positive direction, says Oman's negotiator. Iran again states that an agreement is close, but at the same time says that an open strait requires the US to compensate Iran for violations of the agreement concluded in June.

data.title: AIK:s revansch – nyförvärvet med två mål
data.description: AIK fick revansch när laget vände och vann mot Örgryte. I sin startdebut gjorde Linus Carlstrand två mål när AIK vann med 4–3.
data.translatedTitle: AIK's revenge - the new acquisition with two goals
data.translatedDescription: AIK got revenge when the team turned around and won against Örgryte. In his starting debut, Linus Carlstrand scored two goals as AIK won 4–3.

data.title: Passionerad precision i en roman som höjer sig skyhögt över det medelmåttiga
data.description: Danska Madame Nielsens roman ”Lamento” handlar om en förälskelse som slocknar när kärleken kväver den. Aase Berg får sin världsbild omkastad.
data.translatedTitle: Passionate precision in a novel that soars above the mediocre
data.translatedDescription: Danish Madame Nielsen's novel "Lamento" is about a crush that goes out when love suffocates it. Aase Berg has his worldview turned upside down.

data.title: Expert: Dödläget i Gaza riskerar att fortsätta i tio år
data.description: Det fredsråd som på Donald Trumps initiativ ska styra och ansvara för återuppbyggnaden av Gaza har tecknat sitt första byggkontrakt. – Ett blygsamt steg framåt i det som länge verkat vara ett dödläge, säger Isabell Schierenbeck, professor vid institutionen för globala studier vid Göteborgs universitet.
data.translatedTitle: Expert: The deadlock in Gaza risks continuing for ten years
data.translatedDescription: The peace council that, on Donald Trump's initiative, will govern and be responsible for the reconstruction of Gaza has signed its first construction contract. - A modest step forward in what has long seemed to be a stalemate, says Isabell Schierenbeck, professor at the department of global studies at the University of Gothenburg.

data.title: Viktor Karlsson: Borde betesfår stoppa Natos bataljoner?
data.description: Upprustningen av Europas försvar skapar målkonflikter mellan naturskydd och säkerhet – men vi ska inte dra den förhastade slutsatsen att de aldrig går att lösa ut.
data.translatedTitle: Viktor Karlsson: Should grazing sheep stop NATO's battalions?
data.translatedDescription: The rearmament of Europe's defense creates conflicting goals between nature conservation and security - but we should not jump to the conclusion that they can never be resolved.

data.title: Grönland ger ”skarp varning” till Trump-kopplat oljeprojekt
data.description: Texasbaserade Greenland Energy, som har flera kopplingar till Donald Trump, planerar att borra efter olja på Grönland. Men en del av förarbetet har skett utan vederbörligt tillstånd vilket har fått den grönländska regeringen att utfärda en skarp varning för den fortsatta verksamheten.
data.translatedTitle: Greenland gives 'sharp warning' to Trump-linked oil project
data.translatedDescription: Texas-based Greenland Energy, which has several ties to Donald Trump, plans to drill for oil in Greenland. But some of the preliminary work has taken place without proper permission, which has caused the Greenlandic government to issue a sharp warning for continued operations.

data.title: En vandring i det poetiska Öland pusslar ihop landskapets alla förbindelser
data.description: Kanske har en nyvaken blick på vår planet som en helhet fått oss att se provinsen och det lokala i ett nytt ljus. Sofia Roberg har läst en ny bok om poeterna som Anna Rydstedt, Lennart Sjögren och Göran Sonnevi rör sig i det öländska landskapet.
data.translatedTitle: A hike in the poetic Öland puzzles all the landscape's connections
data.translatedDescription: Perhaps a fresh look at our planet as a whole has made us see the province and the local in a new light. Sofia Roberg has read a new book about the poets Anna Rydstedt, Lennart Sjögren and Göran Sonnevi moving in the Öland landscape.

data.title: SD-ledaren: ”Det pratas väldigt lite om behovet av våra väljare”
data.description: Jimmie Åkesson säger att det ofta glöms bort att hans väljare haft en aversion mot Liberalerna. Även SD-väljare måste hållas nöjda – även om det skrämmer bort borgerliga väljare. – Sverigedemokraterna måste också få vara Sverigedemokraterna, säger Åkesson på turné i norra Sverige.
data.translatedTitle: The SD leader: "There is very little talk about the needs of our voters"
data.translatedDescription: Jimmie Åkesson says that it is often forgotten that his voters had an aversion to the Liberals. SD voters also have to be kept happy – even if it scares bourgeois voters away. - The Sweden Democrats must also be allowed to be the Sweden Democrats, says Åkesson on tour in northern Sweden.

data.title: Sopranen Christina Nilsson: ”Jag har inte levt en minut utan sorgen”
data.description: I morgon uppträder Christina Nilsson på den stora gratiskonserten Filharmonikerna i det gröna vid Sjöhistoriska i Stockholm. DN pratar med världssopranen om kampen för att få flytta hemifrån som 15-åring, kärleken till popmusik och hur man gör för att inte gå vilse bakom scenen på Metropolitan i New York.
data.translatedTitle: Soprano Christina Nilsson: "I haven't lived a minute without sadness"
data.translatedDescription: Tomorrow, Christina Nilsson will perform at the big free concert The Philharmonic in the Green at Sjöhistoriska in Stockholm. DN talks to the world soprano about the struggle to move away from home as a 15-year-old, the love of pop music and how to avoid getting lost backstage at the Metropolitan in New York.

data.title: Maria Gunther: I Washington fortsätter kriget mot vetenskap och forskare
data.description: Donald Trump drömmer om ”en ny guldålder för vetenskapen”. Men stora anslag dras in, hela forskningsfält slaktas, forskning politiseras och häxjakten på Anthony Fauci och andra forskare fortsätter.
data.translatedTitle: Maria Gunther: In Washington, the war against science and scientists continues
data.translatedDescription: Donald Trump dreams of "a new golden age for science". But large grants are withdrawn, entire fields of research are slaughtered, research is politicized and the witch hunt for Anthony Fauci and other scientists continues.

data.title: Johan Croneman: Svårt att hålla tillbaka tårarna när Rosenqvist gör det som inte ska gå att göra
data.description: DN:s sport-i-tv-krönikör Johan Croneman har sett Viaplays dokumentär om Felix Rosenqvists dramatiska seger i racingklassikerna Indy 500. ”Det är fint, det är spännande, det är rörande – dessutom”, skriver han.
data.translatedTitle: Johan Croneman: It's hard to hold back the tears when Rosenqvist does what shouldn't be done
data.translatedDescription: DN's sport-i-tv columnist Johan Croneman has seen Viaplay's documentary about Felix Rosenqvist's dramatic victory in the racing classics Indy 500. "It's nice, it's exciting, it's touching - besides," he writes.

data.title: Plagiatskandal skakar Cambridge – professorer kräver utredning
data.description: Akademiker vid Cambridge kräver en oberoende utredning av skandalen kring professorn Jason Arday. Kraven växer efter anklagelser om plagiat, bristande granskning och frågor om hur universitetet hanterat affären.
data.translatedTitle: Plagiarism scandal shakes Cambridge – professors demand investigation
data.translatedDescription: Cambridge academics are calling for an independent investigation into the scandal surrounding Professor Jason Arday. The demands grow following accusations of plagiarism, lack of review and questions about how the university handled the affair.

data.title: Osynlig evolution – stora uppdateringar av BYD Atto 3
data.description: Massor av effekt, fyrhjulsdrift, höjd laddeffekt och bättre interiör borde väl kunna få oss alla på fall? Men hur stor skillnad gör det för BYD Atto 3 som nu tar steget till Evo.
data.translatedTitle: Invisible evolution – major updates to BYD Atto 3
data.translatedDescription: Lots of power, four-wheel drive, increased charging power and a better interior should be able to make us all fall for it, right? But how big of a difference does it make for the BYD Atto 3, which now makes the step up to the Evo.

data.title: Skarp och subversiv utställning av Superflex
data.description: Den danska konstnärstrion Superflex är aktuell på Arken museum for samtidskunst utanför Köpenhamn. Dan Jönsson imponeras av deras stora, myllrande retrospektiv med en verkkatalog som är både konsekvent och uppfinningsrik.
data.translatedTitle: Sharp and subversive exhibition of Superflex
data.translatedDescription: The Danish artist trio Superflex is current at the Arken museum for contemporary art outside Copenhagen. Dan Jönsson is impressed by their large, teeming retrospective with a work catalog that is both consistent and inventive.

data.title: Leif Zern: Filosofen Edgar Morin var en svuren fiende till slappt vanetänkande
data.description: Den franske filosofen Edgar Morin blev hela 104 år gammal. Han var inte rädd för att ändra uppfattning och skrev lika gärna om filmstjärnor som idépolitik. Jag vet ingen samtida tänkare som har så mycket att säga i dessa tider, skriver Leif Zern.
data.translatedTitle: Leif Zern: The philosopher Edgar Morin was a sworn enemy of lax habitual thinking
data.translatedDescription: The French philosopher Edgar Morin lived to be 104 years old. He wasn't afraid to change his mind and wrote as much about movie stars as ideological politics. I know of no contemporary thinker who has so much to say in these times, writes Leif Zern.

data.title: Lånebok återlämnad efter 150 år
data.description: Biblioteket i australiska Kiama har fått tillbaka boken ”The Antiquities of Athens” 150 år efter att den lånades ut. Förseningsavgiften på cirka 190 000 kronor har avskrivits. – Den har hamnat på en meningsfull plats där den kan delas med omvärlden, säger bibliotekschefen Michelle Hudson till ABC.
data.translatedTitle: Loan book returned after 150 years
data.translatedDescription: The library in Kiama, Australia has received the book "The Antiquities of Athens" back 150 years after it was loaned out. The late fee of approximately SEK 190,000 has been written off. - It has ended up in a meaningful place where it can be shared with the outside world, says library director Michelle Hudson to ABC.

data.title: Baba Stiltz: Jag skulle vilja återfödas som en hyresrätt
data.description: ”Hamlet”. Så svarade Marcel Proust på frågan om sin fiktiva favorithjälte i en sorts Mina vänner-bok som var populär i slutet av 1800-talet. Efter hans död hittades boken med författarens svar och med tiden har formen fått hans namn: The Proust questionnaire, som till exempel är ett stående inslag i amerikanska tidningen Vanity Fair. I DN kallar vi dem Proustfrågorna och i dag svarar musikern och producenten Baba Stiltz.
data.translatedTitle: Baba Stiltz: I would like to be reborn as a tenement
data.translatedDescription: "Hamlet". This is how Marcel Proust answered the question about his favorite fictional hero in a kind of My Friends book that was popular at the end of the 19th century. After his death, the book with the author's answers was found and over time the form has been given his name: The Proust questionnaire, which is, for example, a permanent feature in the American magazine Vanity Fair. In DN we call them the Proust questions and today the musician and producer Baba Stiltz answers them.

data.title: Arvet kom vid olika tid i livet – så användes pengarna

data.translatedTitle: The inheritance came at different times in life - that's how the money was used

data.title: Utdrag ur Per Svenssons postuma bok: ”Läkaren svarar att det rör sig om månader”

data.title: Arvet kommer när det behövs som minst

data.translatedTitle: The inheritance comes when it is needed the least

data.translatedDescription: Stomach growling? Feeling empty? There are many processes behind hunger that tell the body that we need more food.
